```md
# AI extensions: tools, confirmation, and evals

Read this when adding `tools[]`, writing `ai.yaml`, deciding whether an AI layer
is worth building at all, or when the user asks why the Suggested Prompts list
under `@your-extension` is empty.

## Table of contents

- [Who can actually use this](#who-can-actually-use-this)
- [When an AI layer is worth it](#when-an-ai-layer-is-worth-it)
- [tools[]](#tools)
- [The tool file](#the-tool-file)
- [Confirmation](#confirmation)
- [ai.yaml](#aiyaml)
- [Evals are the Suggested Prompts](#evals-are-the-suggested-prompts)
- [Running evals](#running-evals)
- [The AI API](#the-ai-api)

---

## Who can actually use this

The documentation and the product disagree, and the disagreement matters because
it decides whether you build the feature at all.

> *"To use AI APIs or AI Extensions, you need to subscribe to Raycast Pro."*
> — developers.raycast.com/ai/getting-started, still live 2026-07-28

That sentence is stale. Raycast Settings → AI shows three other ways in:

| Path | What it looks like in Settings → AI |
| --- | --- |
| Free allowance | `Try AI — N Messages Left \| x% Used` |
| Custom Providers | *"Add custom providers or use your local LLM by editing the `providers.yaml` file"* — routed direct to the provider, billed at their rates. GitHub Copilot is listed. |
| Local models | *"Locally downloaded AI models via Ollama are supported"*, with an Ollama host and model picker |
| Raycast Pro | unlimited messages |

So **do not reason about subscriptions in code, and do not skip the feature
because of Pro.** There is exactly one correct check, and it is a runtime
capability test:

\```ts
import { AI, environment } from "@raycast/api";

if (!environment.canAccess(AI)) {
  // degrade — do not throw, do not show a paywall you cannot verify
}
\```

Documented behaviour: *"You can check if a user has access to the API using
`environment.canAccess(AI)`"* and *"If the user doesn't wish to get access, the
API call will throw an error."*

`canAccess` is only needed when **your own code** calls `AI.ask`. A `tools[]`
entry is invoked *by* Raycast AI, so the user has already cleared whatever gate
applies before your function runs — a tool never needs to check.

**Windows: undocumented.** Neither the changelog nor raycast.com/windows says
whether AI Extensions work there. Do not add `Windows` to `platforms` on the
strength of a tool layer without testing it. See `cross-platform.md`.

## When an AI layer is worth it

The honest test is whether you already did the work. If Workflow B's transport
returns structured data, a tool is a fifteen-line wrapper and the remaining
effort is prompt-shaped, not code-shaped:

\```ts
export default async function tool() {
  return await read({ group: undefined });   // the transport you already have
}
\```

That is the whole read-side tool. Propose one whenever:

- the extension already parses its backend into typed objects, **and**
- a user question would otherwise require reading a list and doing arithmetic
  ("how far through is each group", "which failures share a cause").

Skip it when the extension is a launcher or a single-action command — there is
nothing for a model to reason over, and a tool that wraps one deterministic
action is worse than the keyboard shortcut for it.

## tools[]

Straight from the live schema at
<https://www.raycast.com/schemas/extension.json>:

\```json
"tools": [
  {
    "name": "list-tasks",
    "title": "List Tasks",
    "description": "Read the queue and return every task with its status, group, and runtime."
  }
]
\```

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | required · pattern `^[a-z0-9-][a-zA-Z0-9-_]*$` · 2–64 chars · **maps to the entry point file**: `list-tasks` → `src/tools/list-tasks.ts` |
| `title` | required · 2–255 · no leading/trailing whitespace |
| `description` | required · **minimum 12 characters** · *"helps users (and other actors like AI) understand what the tool does"* |
| `icon` | optional · 512×512 PNG in `assets/`, `@light`/`@dark` suffixes supported · inherits the extension icon |
| `keywords`, `preferences` | optional, same shapes as a command's |
| `functionalities` | optional · enum `"AI attachment provider"` \| `"AI tool"` · restricts where the tool may be used. Omit unless you mean to restrict. |

The description is **prompt engineering, not documentation** — it is the primary
signal Raycast AI uses to pick between your tools. Two tools whose descriptions
differ only in adjectives will be chosen between at random.

Tools do not appear in root search. They are reached with `@extension-name` in
Quick AI or AI Chat, or from the *Ask …* item at the top of the extension.

## The tool file

\```ts
// src/tools/list-tasks.ts
type Input = {
  /**
   * Only return tasks in this group. Omit for every group.
   * Group names are case-sensitive and come from `list-groups`.
   */
  group?: string;
  /** Only return tasks in this state. */
  status?: "queued" | "running" | "success" | "failed";
};

export default async function tool(input: Input) {
  const state = await read({ group: input.group });
  return state.tasks.filter((t) => !input.status || t.status === input.status);
}
\```

- **A tool takes exactly one object.** *"A tool expects a single object as its
  input."* Positional parameters are not a thing here.
- **JSDoc on the `Input` fields IS the parameter schema.** *"To better teach AI
  how to use your tools, you can add descriptions as JSDoc comments."* An
  undocumented field is a field the model guesses at. Say where legal values come
  from, not just what the field means.
- **Prefer a string union over `string`** for anything enumerable. It lands in
  the generated schema and stops the model inventing `"pending"`.
- **Return data, not prose.** The model does the writing; a tool that returns a
  formatted sentence throws away the structure the model needed.
- **Strip secrets on the way out**, exactly as at the cache boundary
  (`data-and-state.md`) — a tool return value goes to a model, and with a Custom
  Provider that model is somebody else's endpoint.

## Confirmation

**There is a confirmation surface inside a tool call.** A tool file may export
one, and Raycast calls it before executing:

\```ts
import { Tool } from "@raycast/api";

export const confirmation: Tool.Confirmation<Input> = async (input) => {
  if (!input.ids?.length) return undefined;      // nothing destructive — skip it
  return {
    style: Tool.Confirmation.Style.Destructive,
    message: `Kill ${input.ids.length} running task(s)? Output is not recoverable.`,
    info: [
      { name: "Group", value: input.group ?? "all" },
      { name: "Tasks", value: input.ids.join(", ") },
    ],
  };
};
\```

The documented signature is
`type Confirmation<T> = (input: T) => Promise<undefined | { … }>`, and it is
*"called before the actual tool is executed"*. Fields: `message`, `info[]` of
`{ name, value }`, `style` (regular or destructive), and `image`.

Two consequences:

- **A destructive tool does not have to be withheld.** The old advice "ship
  read-only first" was based on this API not existing. Gate it instead.
- **`undefined` skips the prompt**, so confirmation can be conditional — free for
  a no-op call, present for a real one. Entries in `info` whose value is
  `undefined` are not rendered, so building it is not fiddly.

`confirmAlert` still does not work here. It renders in the Raycast window, and a
tool call is not guaranteed to have one — `Tool.Confirmation` is the replacement,
not an addition.

## ai.yaml

`instructions` and `evals` live under the manifest's `ai` key, but the docs
recommend pulling them out: *"we recommend you to use a `ai.yaml` file in the
root of your extension next to the `package.json` file."* The YAML holds the
**contents** of the `ai` object, not an `ai:` wrapper:

\```yaml
# ai.yaml
instructions: |
  Never restart, kill, or clean anything unless the user explicitly asks.
  Task ids are only unique within a group — always report the group too.
  When the queue is empty, say so plainly instead of describing the schema.

evals:
  - input: "@pueue What's running right now, and how long has each one been going?"
  - input: "@pueue Why did my failed tasks fail? Read the logs — don't fix anything yet."
  - input: "@pueue Which group has the most failures, and do they share a cause?"
\```

The equivalent inside `package.json` is identical in shape:

\```json
"ai": { "instructions": "…", "evals": [{ "input": "@pueue …" }] }
\```

Use one or the other, not both. `ai.yaml` wins on diff noise the moment
`instructions` grows past a line, which it will.

`instructions` is *"added as a system message whenever the extension is
mentioned"* — extension-wide, and it applies to every tool. Put the invariants
there (what is destructive, what identifiers mean, what never to do unasked) and
keep per-tool semantics in the tool `description` and the `Input` JSDoc.

## Evals are the Suggested Prompts

This is the part nobody finds by reading the API reference. From the docs:

> *"They are also used as suggested prompts for the user to learn how to make the
> most out of your AI Extension."*

The `evals[].input` strings are what render under **Suggested Prompts** when a
user types `@your-extension`. `usedAsExample` controls it — *"Whether the eval
can be used as an example in Raycast (default `true`)"*. So:

- **An extension with `tools[]` and no `evals` shows an empty prompt list.** The
  tools work; the user just has no idea what to ask. That is the single highest
  ratio of perceived quality to effort in the whole AI surface.
- **Write them as prompts, not as test fixtures.** They are user-facing copy.
  The full form is a test:

  \```json
  {
    "input": "@pueue what are my failed tasks",
    "mocks": { "list-tasks": [{ "id": 3, "status": "failed", "group": "default" }] },
    "expected": [{ "callsTool": "list-tasks" }]
  }
  \```

  but the schema requires only `input`. A bare `input` is a valid eval and a
  valid suggested prompt — there is no reason to ship zero of them.
- **Set `usedAsExample: false` on the ugly ones.** Regression cases with
  contrived phrasing are worth keeping as tests and embarrassing as UI.
- Cover the read paths first, and phrase at least one to establish the boundary:
  *"Read the logs — don't fix anything yet."* teaches the user that this
  extension can also write, and teaches the model what restraint looks like.

Matchers available in `expected`: `callsTool`, `includes`, `matches`,
`meetsCriteria`, `eq`, and the combinators `and`, `or`, `not`.

## Running evals

\```bash
npx ray evals
\```

**This is a manual step, not a gate step.** It needs AI access and network, so it
cannot join `tsc --noEmit && ray lint && ray build` in a `just check` recipe that
has to work offline and on a fresh clone. Run it when tool descriptions or
`instructions` change — those are the only edits that can regress tool
*selection*, and nothing else in the toolchain tests selection at all.

## The AI API

Distinct from tools: `AI.ask` is *your* code calling a model.

\```ts
import { AI, environment } from "@raycast/api";

if (!environment.canAccess(AI)) return fallback();

const answer = await AI.ask("Summarise this build log:\n" + log, {
  model: AI.Model["Anthropic_Claude_4.5_Haiku"],
  creativity: 0,        // 0–2
  signal: abort.signal,
});
\```

The return value is a `Promise<string>` **and** an `EventEmitter` — subscribe to
`"data"` to stream into a `Detail` as it arrives rather than blocking on the
whole answer.

Pin a `model` only when the task needs a specific capability; the enum churns
fast (it gained several entries between Raycast releases), and an id that
disappears is a runtime failure in a code path users rarely hit. Omitting `model`
lets Raycast pick, which also respects a user's Custom Provider or Ollama choice.

`AI.ask` is the wrong tool when the user is already in Quick AI — that is what
`tools[]` is for. Reach for it when the extension itself needs a model in the
middle of a deterministic flow, and give the user a way to see the raw input.

```

you should use. Leave it — fighting Raycast's own recommended constant is worse
than a dev-mode duplicate. Everything else in this table, avoid.

**3. `Keyboard.Shortcut.Common.*` — free to use, but check the actual keys.**

| Constant | macOS |
| --- | --- || `Copy` | `⌘⇧C` |
| `CopyDeeplink` | `⌘⇧C` |
| `CopyName` | `⌘⇧.` |
| `CopyPath` | `⌘⇧,` |
| `Save` | `⌘S` |
| `Duplicate` | **`⌘D`** |
| `Edit` | `⌘E` |
| `MoveUp` / `MoveDown` | `⌘⇧↑` / `⌘⇧↓` |
| `New` | `⌘N` |
| `Open` | `⌘O` |
| `OpenWith` | `⌘⇧O` |
| `Pin` | `⌘⇧P` |
| `Refresh` | `⌘R` |
| `Remove` | **`⌃X`** |
| `RemoveAll` | `⌃⇧X` |
| `ToggleQuickLook` | `⌘Y` |

The two in bold are the ones people guess wrong. `Remove` is **not** `⌘⌫`, and
`Duplicate` is **not** `⌘⇧D`. Both were written into a README from memory and
were wrong for months, because nothing checks documentation against bindings.
If you list shortcuts in a README, copy them from this table or from
`developers.raycast.com/api-reference/keyboard` — not from what you remember
typing.

Note also that `Pin` is `⌘⇧P`. Reusing that key for something else (a Pause
action, say) is legal and works, but the moment a panel gains a real pin action
you have a silent conflict.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
Looking at the actual ray CLI source code, I'm finding that the file resolution order is `ai.json` → `ai.json5` → `ai.yaml` → `ai.yml`, with the first match winning. This means there are four accepted filenames, not just one, and JSON variants take precedence over YAML — a gotcha that's not documented anywhere, so leaving an old `ai.json` file around would silently shadow your `ai.yaml` configuration.

The parsed AI file gets merged into the manifest using a shallow merge where the file's values override the package.json `ai` key, so any keys you define in the file win out while keys only in package.json survive the merge.

Tool schema extraction happens at build time through the TypeScript compiler, which looks for `src/tools/<name>.ts` or `.tsx` files and requires a default exported function (throwing an error if it's missing). The build enforces that tools have at most one parameter, reads the JSDoc from the default export as the tool's instructions, detects a `confirmation` export to set that flag, and extracts the input schema from the parameter type and output schema from the return type.

The `ray develop` command watches `ai.json`, `ai.yml`, and `ai.yaml` files but notably not `ai.json5` despite reading it — an asymmetry worth noting. Hidden flags like `--print-tool-schemas`, `--print-instructions`, and `--print-tool-calls` exist on `ray develop`, with tool calls printing enabled by default and logged as `__tool_input__` and `__tool_output__` along with the tool name and whether it's the confirmation or the tool itself.

The esbuild target is set to `node22.22.2`, confirming the @types/node version. I'm thinking this is the kind of implementation detail worth documenting in ai-extensions.md, and I should also check the `ray evals` flags and how the build resolves tool names to files.

## The manifest side

```json
{ "name": "queue-menu", "title": "Queue Menu Bar", "mode": "menu-bar", "interval": "1m" }
```

- **`platforms: ["macOS"]` becomes mandatory** at the top level. Menu bar is
  macOS-only.
- **`interval` is manifest-only.** A preference cannot change it, because Raycast
  renders its own refresh-interval control in the command's settings. Shipping an
  interval preference would be a lie.
- The docs contradict themselves on the floor — the background-refresh page says
  `10s`, the manifest page says `1m`. **Use `1m`.** It is what shipped
  extensions use and it is the safe value.
- **Background refresh is off by default for store installs.** Until the user
  runs the command once or enables it in settings, a freshly installed menu-bar

/**
 * AI tool: __TOOL_NAME__
 *
 * The filename MUST equal the tools[].name entry in package.json.
 * `ray build` runs tsc over this file and derives the tool's JSON schema from
 * the types below — so the annotations here are the contract, not decoration.
 *
 * This JSDoc becomes the tool's `instructions`. Say what the tool is for and
 * what it must never do; leave parameter semantics to the Input fields.
 */

// import { Action, Tool } from "@raycast/api";

type Input = {
  /**
   * Describe every field. An undocumented field is one the model guesses at.
   * Say where legal values come from, not just what the field means.
   */
  query?: string;
  /**
   * Prefer a string union over `string` for anything enumerable — it lands in
   * the extracted schema and stops the model inventing values.
   */
  status?: "active" | "done";
};

/**
 * The default export must be a function taking AT MOST ONE parameter.
 * `Tools should have at most one parameter (has 2)` is a build error, not a
 * runtime one.
 *
 * Annotate the return type. It is extracted as the tool's `output` schema, so
 * anything that widens to `any` ships a useless one. Return data, not prose —
 * the model does the writing.
 */
export default async function tool(input: Input): Promise<unknown[]> {
  void input;
  throw new Error("__TOOL_NAME__ is not implemented");
}

/**
 * Uncomment for anything that mutates. Raycast calls this BEFORE the tool and
 * skips the prompt entirely when it returns undefined — so a confirmation can
 * be conditional and costs nothing on a harmless call.
 *
 * Note `style` is `Action.Style`, reused. There is no Tool-local style enum.

# AI configuration for __NAME__
#
# This file holds the CONTENTS of the manifest's `ai` key — no `ai:` wrapper.
# Four filenames are accepted and the FIRST match wins: ai.json, ai.json5,
# ai.yaml, ai.yml. Keep exactly one; a stale ai.json silently shadows this file.
# `ray develop` hot-reloads ai.yaml, ai.yml and ai.json — but not ai.json5.

# Injected as a system message whenever the extension is mentioned with @__NAME__.
# Put the invariants here: what is destructive, what identifiers mean, what must
# never happen unasked. Per-tool semantics belong in the tool description and the
# Input JSDoc, not here.
instructions: |
  Never mutate anything unless the user explicitly asks for it.
  Prefer reporting what you found over speculating about causes.

# Evals are integration tests AND the Suggested Prompts list shown under
# @__NAME__. Only `input` is required, so there is no excuse for shipping zero:
# an extension with tools and no evals looks empty to every new user.
#
# Set usedAsExample: false on regression cases with contrived phrasing — worth
# keeping as a test, embarrassing as UI. It defaults to true.
#
# Run them with `npx ray evals` (needs AI access and network, so it is a manual
# step, not part of `just check`).
evals:
  - input: "@__NAME__ Give me an overview of everything. Don't change anything."
  - input: "@__NAME__ What's active right now, and how long has each one been going?"
  - input: "@__NAME__ What failed, and why? Read the details — don't fix anything yet."

```

113	i=0

116	  cmode=$(printf '%s' "$spec" | cut -d: -f2)

123	    "") die "--command \"$spec\": missing MODE (use NAME:view, NAME:no-view, or NAME:menu-bar)" ;;
124	    *)  die "--command \"$spec\": MODE must be view, no-view, or menu-bar; got \"$cmode\"" ;;
125	  esac

127	  CMD_NAMES[i]="$cname"; CMD_MODES[i]="$cmode"; CMD_TITLES[i]="$ctitle"

140	[ "$HARNESS" -eq 1 ] && FILES[${#FILES[@]}]="src/lib/dev-check.ts"

144	  for e in "$@"; do out="${out}${out:+,}\"$(printf '%s' "$e" | sed -e 's/\\/\\\\/g' -e 's/"/\\"/g')\""; done
145	  printf '[%s]' "$out"
146	}

148	CMD_JSON_LIST=""
149	i=0
150	while [ $i -lt ${#CMD_NAMES[@]} ]; do
151	  CMD_JSON_LIST="${CMD_JSON_LIST}${CMD_JSON_LIST:+,}{\"name\":\"${CMD_NAMES[$i]}\",\"mode\":\"${CMD_MODES[$i]}\"}"
152	  i=$((i + 1))
153	done
154	
155	NEXT_STEPS=("cd $DIR && npm install"
156	            "npm run build   # this is what GENERATES raycast-env.d.ts"
157	            "just check      # tsc --noEmit, verify, ray lint, ray build"
158	            "npm run dev, then open the command FROM RAYCAST ROOT SEARCH, not the dev console"
159	            "replace assets/extension-icon.png — the placeholder is rejected by review")
160

165	}

167	if [ "$DRY_RUN" -eq 1 ]; then

171	fi

180	mkdir -p "$DIR/src/lib" "$DIR/assets" "$DIR/metadata"

182	COMMANDS_JSON=""

184	while [ $i -lt ${#CMD_NAMES[@]} ]; do
185	  entry="    {
186	      \"name\": \"${CMD_NAMES[$i]}\",
187	      \"title\": \"${CMD_TITLES[$i]}\",
188	      \"description\": \"Open the ${CMD_TITLES[$i]} command.\",
189	      \"mode\": \"${CMD_MODES[$i]}\""
190	  [ "${CMD_MODES[$i]}" = "menu-bar" ] && entry="$entry,
191	      \"interval\": \"1m\""

205	subst() { # template destination

216	      print
217	    }' "$1" > "$2"
218	}

248	  <rect x="2" y="11" width="8"  height="2" rx="1" fill="black"/>
249	</svg>
250	SVG
251	fi

255	.build/
256	.raycast-swift-build/
257	dist/

285	cat > "$DIR/CHANGELOG.md" <<EOF

288	## [Initial Version] - {PR_MERGE_DATE}
289	
290	- First release.
291	EOF

293	{
294	  printf '# %s\n\n%s\n\n## Setup\n\n' "$TITLE" "$DESCRIPTION"

297	  printf '   default PATH — Raycast runs under launchd with no shell rc, so a bare\n'

316	export default function Command() {
317	  return (
318	    <List searchBarPlaceholder="Search…">
319	      <List.Item
320	        title="$t"
321	        actions={
322	          <ActionPanel>
323	            <Action.CopyToClipboard title="Copy" content="$t" />
324	          </ActionPanel>

330	EOF
331	      ;;

336	// A no-view command exports an async function, NOT a React component. There is

type Input = {

  ids: number[];
};

  void input;
}

};

2. Pro-gating —— 改成 `environment.canAccess(AI)` 是唯一正確判斷，並列出四條取得管道。文件那句 "you need to subscribe to Raycast Pro" 有引用並標為已過時。

## 三個計畫外的發現（都已寫進 skill）

- **schema 和 changelog 對 `platforms` 預設值說法相反**：changelog 說 `["macOS"]`，live JSON schema 說 "assumed to be available on all platforms"，而且它不在 `required` 裡。結論改成「一律明確宣告」，並加 `platforms-declared` warn。
- **AI 設定檔有四個名字，先找到先贏**：`ai.json` → `ai.json5` → `ai.yaml` → `ai.yml`（從 `ray` CLI 的 `readAIFile` 讀出來的）。留一個舊的 `ai.json` 會靜默蓋掉你在編輯的 `ai.yaml`。多加了 `ai-file-unique` 檢查。順帶：`ray develop` 不 watch `ai.json5`。
- **`Keyboard.Shortcut` 的 per-platform 形式兩個分支都是必填**，小寫 `windows` 已 deprecated 但仍能編譯 —— 這比 changelog 的範例精確。

## 兩處我偏離了原計畫

- **`ui-patterns.md` 沒加 Windows 欄位**。`Keyboard.Shortcut.Common.*` 的 Windows 綁定是在 Raycast app 內解析的，`@raycast/api` typings 只標成 `Shortcut`，本機查不到值。與其編一欄，我改成明說「查不到，所以更該用這些常數」。
- **`--tool` 名稱驗證用 schema 真實 pattern**（`^[a-z0-9-][a-zA-Z0-9-_]*$`, 2–64）而非計畫寫的 kebab-case —— 後者會誤拒合法的 `listTasks`。

## 一個實測到的反例

我在 reference 初稿寫「return type 會被抽成 `output` schema」（CLI 原始碼確實有這條路徑）。實測 `Promise<T[]>`、`Promise<{…}>`、`Promise<unknown[]>` 三種形狀在 1.104.23 **都沒有產生 `output` key**。已改寫成實測結果並註明版本，template 的註解也一併修掉。

## 驗證

`ray lint`（`CI=true`）對 `platforms: ["macOS","Windows"]` + `tools[]` + `ai.yaml` 的 scaffold 全綠 —— 這是對 live schema 最強的證明。`tsc --noEmit`、`ray build`、`ray build -e dist` 皆過。readiness 的 5 個新檢查各自用負向 fixture 逼進 fail/warn 狀態驗過，整體 exit 4 正確。repo 的 `make validate` 三關全過。

過程中順帶實證了 skill 既有的 lockfile gotcha：`CI=true npx ray lint` 真的因為 `registry.npmmirror.com` 而 fail，照 skill 寫的 host 替換法修好後就過了。

Summary of useAI (from @raycast/utils)

Signature (paraphrased)
- useAI(prompt: string, options?): returns AsyncState<string> plus a revalidate() method.

What it does (short verbatim quote)
- "Hook which asks the AI to answer a prompt and returns the [AsyncState] corresponding to the execution of the query." 

Options (paraphrased; each description condensed from the source)
- creativity: number (0–2) to control answer creativity (lower for concrete tasks, higher for open-ended ones).
- model: selects which AI model to use.
- stream: boolean; when true, data is streamed as it arrives; when false, data updates only after the whole answer is received.
- execute: boolean (from usePromise options) — if false, the hook is defined but will not run until you enable execution.
- onError: callback(error) invoked on execution failure (default logs and shows a failure toast).
- onData: callback(data) invoked on successful execution.
- onWillExecute: callback(args) invoked before execution starts.
- failureToastOptions: partial customization for failure toast title, message, and primaryAction.

Short verbatim option text (<=125 chars)
- "options.creativity is a number between 0 and 2 to control the creativity of the answer."

Return values (paraphrased)
- data: the AI response string (or undefined initially).
- isLoading: boolean indicating loading state.
- error: Error when execution fails.
- revalidate(): call to run the same prompt again.

Short verbatim return text (<=125 chars)
- "revalidate is a method to manually call the function with the same arguments again."

Example (paraphrased)
- Import and call the hook with a prompt; render the streamed result and loading state in a Detail.
- Verbatim line from the example (<=125 chars):
  "const { data, isLoading } = useAI(\"Suggest 5 jazz songs\");"

AsyncState shapes (paraphrased)
- Initial: isLoading true/false, data undefined, error undefined.
- Success: isLoading false, data string, error undefined.
- Error: isLoading false, data undefined, error Error.
- Reloading: isLoading true, data string|undefined, error Error|undefined.

Notes
- Quoted phrases above are taken directly from the documented page; all other wording is a concise restatement.

```text
## Which storage for which value

| Need | Use | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remote data, want it on screen instantly next launch | `useCachedPromise` | disk-backed, keyed by the argument array |
| Remote data, no cache wanted | `usePromise` | same shape, nothing persisted |
| View state read synchronously during render | `useCachedState` | sync; survives relaunch |
| A value another **command** must read | `LocalStorage` | async; the only cross-command channel |
| Ad-hoc key/value from non-hook code | `Cache` | what `useCachedPromise` writes to |

`useCachedState` and `LocalStorage` are not interchangeable. A filter the current
view needs during its first render must be `useCachedState`; the last-used group
that a `no-view` sibling command reads must be `LocalStorage`.
```
</details></tool-use>

Merged. `main` is at `58b3fb0`, one commit ahead of `origin/main`, branch deleted. (The only dirty file is the live SpecStory transcript, which keeps appending as we talk.)

## Workflow: it didn't finish — it was interrupted

`research:toolfile` never returned; its transcript ends with `[Request interrupted by user]`. So Verify and Synthesize never ran, and **nothing in it was adversarially checked**. But it had done ~217 turns of real empirical probing first, which was salvageable.

I treated all of it as leads, not facts, and re-ran the load-bearing ones myself.

## What I verified and folded in

The big one — **tool schema extraction is the single thing `ray build` actually enforces**. Unsupported types abort the build with `Error: extracting tool schemas failed`, in the same dev build that cheerfully ships a `TS2345` everywhere else. Measured, one probe tool per case:

| Works | Hard build error |
|---|---|
| `string` `number` `boolean` `string[]` | `any`, `unknown` |
| string unions → `enum` | `1\|2` and `"x"\|1` — *numeric unions are not enums here* |
| optional fields, nested object literals | `A & B` intersections |
| type aliases | `Pick` / `Partial` → `Could not resolve type Pick` |

And two that are neither — **silently wrong**:

- **`interface Input extends Base {}` extracts as `{}`.** No error, build succeeds, model gets a tool that looks like it takes no arguments. `interface Input { b: string }` is fine; only *inheritance* is dropped.
- **JSDoc only counts on its own line.** `/** doc */ field: string` on one line yields no `description` at all — looks documented in the editor, invisible to the model.

Also: the param type needn't be named `Input` (inline anonymous works), and `confirmation` is detected in all five export forms including HoC-wrapped — I'd mis-read a truncated line earlier as showing HoC failing; the full line says `c_hoc confirmation=true`, so my original claim stood.

One I found myself while testing the template: a bare `@word` in tool JSDoc gets parsed as a JSDoc tag, so my own `@raycast/api` came back as `@raycast /api` in the extracted instructions. Fixed and documented.

## Where the workflow and I disagreed

Its probe reported `Pick`/`Partial` producing *empty properties*; mine got a *hard build error*. Likely because it called the extractor directly while I went through `ray build`. I documented my result, since the build is what anyone actually runs.

## Still worth knowing

That workflow cost ~220k tokens across three agents and produced no synthesized output. The two completed sweeps were genuinely useful as a lead generator — `emoji-kitchen` and `cursor-agents` were finds I wouldn't have made — but every claim I shipped from it, I re-measured first.

Reminder from earlier: the installed copy at `InfoSummarizer/.claude/skills/raycast-extension-dev/` is still the old 6-reference version.
